title: Length-cluster eviction study and GPU slab reclamation for continuous batcher
creator: Priya Menon
description: Problem statement: Mixed prompt/response workloads cause the continuous batcher to hold long-lived KV entries and large GPU slabs for a small fraction of requests, increasing memory pressure and tail latency. Goal: evaluate length-clustering heuristics combined with a tiered eviction policy and aggressive GPU slab reclamation to reduce peak memory usage and 95th/99th latency without hurting mean throughput.
background: We see recurring OOM and high tail latency on multi-tenant pods when conversing workloads mix short system prompts (<=32 tokens) with long streaming responses (>1024 tokens).
Existing rules are time-based and single-threshold eviction which causes either premature eviction (quality regressions) or stale hold of large KV slices (memory blowup).
Previous tickets (ENG-67214, ENG-52311) added length-aware packing but did not explore clustering or GPU slab reclamation strategies.
hypothesis: Clustering incoming requests by prompt+expected-response length and assigning them to 'length lanes' will keep KV lifetimes predictable and allow tighter per-lane eviction thresholds.

A two-tier eviction policy (lane-local soft eviction + global hard eviction) plus cooperative GPU slab reclamation for cold lanes will reduce max resident GPU memory by >20% and reduce 99th latency by 10-15% on mixed workloads.
Small short-request lanes should be allowed to be coalesced aggressively; long-request lanes get larger KV reservations but isolated slots to avoid fragmenting slabs.
GPU slab reclamation that merges adjacent cold allocations and compacts free spans during low-util periods will lower fragmentation-related OOMs.
We will not degrade tail-quality for priority customers; experiments will include a quality smoke test set.
acceptance_criteria: Peak GPU memory per-pod reduced by >=20% on representative mixed workload trace
99th percentile latency reduced by >=10% without increasing 50th percentile latency by more than 5%
No regressions on unit quality tests (prompt/response fidelity) for 95% of eval prompts
Feature gated and rolloutable: can be enabled per-model and per-customer via config
Automated canary dashboard created showing memory, 50/95/99 latency, KV hit-rate, and quality regressions.
design_notes: Introduce a length clustering stage in the scheduler that maps requests to discrete lanes: micro (<=64), short (65-256), medium (257-1024), long (>1024).
Per-lane soft TTL for KV cache (adaptive based on observed reuse) and a global hard TTL to bound residency.
Implement lane-aware slot reservation so that long lanes reserve contiguous slab regions to avoid interleaved fragmentation.
Add a GPU slab compaction hook that runs opportunistically when GPU utilization < 30% for a sustained window and merges small free spans.
Expose config knobs: lane-bucket-boundaries, soft-ttl-scale, hard-ttl-ms, compaction-min-free-frag, compaction-util-threshold.
Metrics: lane-resident-bytes, lane-kv-entries, lane-hit-rate, slab-fragmentation-ratio, compaction-count, compaction-duration.
Plan safe fallback: requests tagged with 'no-evict' by higher-priority customers will bypass compaction and use conservative TTLs.
test_plan: Offline replay of production traces (7 days) across 3 instance classes (A100-80GB, A10-24GB, V100-32GB) with and without changes.
Microbench harness for synthetic skewed-dialogs: 70% short prompts / 30% long responses at 500 RPS per-pod.
A/B canary on 2 pods in staging for 48 hours with traffic shadowed from production; compare memory/latency/quality metrics.
Quality smoke: 200 canonical prompts with similarity/delta checks against baseline outputs after eviction events.
Run fault injection to ensure compaction does not deadlock or cause request stalls (timeout tolerance checks).
risks: Compaction may introduce CPU/GPU stalls if not scheduled carefully — must be throttled and cancelable.
Over-aggressive soft TTL tuning could evict useful KV entries and increase token compute cost (quality regressions).
Lane boundaries may not generalize to all workloads; need a feedback loop to adjust buckets.
Complexity of slab coalescing across different CUDA allocator behaviors could cause platform-specific bugs.
Rollback must be trivial — provide feature flag and per-instance disable.
implementation_steps: 1) Add length-clustering filter in scheduler and wire lane labels into request context (ENG-84763-1).
2) Implement per-lane metadata and soft TTL logic in KV cache (ENG-84763-2).
3) Modify slot allocator to support contiguous reservations for long lanes (ENG-84763-3).
4) Prototype GPU slab compaction hook with safe preemption and metrics (ENG-84763-4).
5) Run offline replay and iterate TTL/bucket boundaries based on telemetry (ENG-84763-5).
6) Canary rollout behind feature flag; monitor canary dashboard and roll forward/rollback as needed (ENG-84763-6).
7) Documentation and console knobs for per-customer configs (ENG-84763-7).
metrics_and_dashboards: New dashboard: 'Length-lane memory & latency' showing lane-resident-bytes, slab-frag-ratio, 50/95/99 latencies per lane.
Alert: slab-frag-ratio > 0.6 and free-bytes < 10% for > 5m triggers P0 page for memory pressure
Experiment tracking: compare baseline vs trial pods with 24h/48h aggregated reports stored in /dashboards/experiments/length-lane.
